extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, legal advocates, agency counsel, and stakeholders preparing comments or litigation concerning EPA rulemaking under the Clean Air Act
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-argument comment opposing EPA’s proposed repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding under CAA §202(a), focusing on doctrinal, statutory-interpretive, and administrative-law standards the Agency must satisfy. Targets how courts should evaluate EPA’s reliance on the major-questions doctrine, statutory text/history, and arbitrary-and-capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Questions Doctrine—history and breadth requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine is limited to cases where both the “history and the breadth” of the authority asserted and the “economic and political significance” of the authority provide reason to hesitate before assuming Congress intended to bestow it. (West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 721.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is reserved for unprecedented and transformative exercises of power; it has never been applied based on economic and political significance alone. Applying it broadly would make the doctrine the rule rather than an extraordinary exception (Brown & Williamson, 529 U.S. at 159). Courts should therefore require evidence of both unheralded history/breadth and novel transformative authority before invoking the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Questions—economic/political significance alone insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has never applied the major-questions doctrine based on the economic and political significance of a purported authority alone; economic and political significance, standing alone, do not trigger the doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broader conception would risk applying the doctrine whenever a regulation is consequential. Agencies and courts must show that the asserted authority’s economic and political consequences are different in kind from other statutory delegations before treating the case as a major question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on agency to show difference-in-kind consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke the major-questions doctrine based on economic/political significance, the agency must demonstrate that the consequences of regulating greenhouse gases under §202(a) are vastly different in kind from regulating other pollutants; it must show that every conceivable exercise of §202(a) authority over GHGs would have extreme consequences different in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough to show that some exercises of the authority could be economically or politically significant; the agency must establish a qualitative difference from other emissions regulations. Historical evidence of prior rules and their impact is relevant and undercuts such a showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of precedent and reliance—must acknowledge and rebut prior findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing to abandon longstanding agency positions or findings, the Agency must acknowledge and explain deviations from its prior factual findings and reasoned analyses; failure to do so renders reliance arbitrary and capricious (Fox, 556 U.S. at 515–16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must engage with and rebut its own extensive prior factual findings about costs, benefits, indirect impacts, grid reliability, battery production, infrastructure timing, and net societal benefits from its 2024 standards and prior rules. Simply asserting new conclusions without addressing earlier analyses is unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to past standards—evidence of adaptiveness and comparable costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical record of prior greenhouse-gas vehicle standards (≈15 years) showing manufacturers adapted and costs fell within ranges Congress accepted undermines claims that GHG regulation under §202(a) is sui generis or unaffordable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and commenters should consider agency findings (e.g., average costs per vehicle comparable to prior rules; operating cost savings outweigh upfront costs; estimated net benefits) when assessing whether a rule presents novel economic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondelegation/intelligible-principle requirement satisfied by §202(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress provided specific direction about when and how to regulate under §202(a); those statutory guardrails satisfy the intelligible-principle requirement, obviating nondelegation concerns without invoking an atextual bar on regulating greenhouse gases (Whitman, 531 U.S. at 473–75).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA advances nondelegation or constitutional-avoidance arguments to restrict §202(a), courts should assess whether the statute’s text, structure, and legislative history supply adequate guidance rather than inventing new textual limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Questions—not a necessary constitutional-avoidance tool here
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if some justices view the major-questions doctrine as a presumption used for constitutional avoidance, application here is unnecessary because the statutory and historical record supports EPA authority and does not present nondelegation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies cannot unilaterally adopt a more aggressive major-questions test for constitutional reasons absent showing that established factors are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear-authorization standard if major questions applied
rubrics_metrics.description: If a court did apply the major-questions doctrine, it requires “clear congressional authorization” for an agency to exercise the claimed power (West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 731).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should look to statutory text, legislative history, and long congressional acquiescence (including Massachusetts and AEP) to determine whether Congress clearly authorized EPA regulation of GHGs under §202(a). Stare decisis principles (Loper Bright) also counsel sustaining established readings unless exceptional circumstances exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEP displacement principle—regulatory authority required to displace federal common law
rubrics_metrics.description: American Electric Power Co. v. Connecticut holds that where a federal statute “speaks directly to the question,” it displaces federal common law; displacement depends on Congress having delegated the decision whether and how to regulate the pollutant to EPA. A finding that EPA lacks §202(a) authority would eliminate the basis for displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot coherently assert it lacks authority under §202(a) while simultaneously claiming the Clean Air Act continues to preempt federal common-law claims for GHG emissions; finalization of a repeal would remove the statutory basis for AEP displacement and potentially reopen common-law claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency requirement—cannot both disclaim authority and claim continued preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency cannot on the one hand argue §202(a) does not authorize GHG regulation and on the other hand insist the CAA still displaces federal common-law suits about GHGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal analyses must be consistent about the consequences of statutory interpretation; commenters should point out and courts should reject attempts to have both results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral effects across the CAA—assess cross-program impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeal of the endangerment finding or holding that §202(a) does not authorize GHG regulation risks undermining displacement under AEP across other statutory programs (e.g., §111 stationary sources, §231 aircraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency and courts must consider how a novel limiting interpretation would ripple across the Act and related regulatory programs; failure to analyze these effects is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory text—§202(a)(1) contains no timing or concurrency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain language of §202(a)(1) establishes no timing or process requirement that an endangerment/contribution finding and emission standards be issued concurrently; the Administrator’s judgment may rely on prior findings when issuing standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the statute neither authorizes nor forbids standalone findings, EPA’s 2009 approach issuing an antecedent endangerment finding was permissible. Commenters and courts should resist reading words like “simultaneous” or “concurrent” into §202 where Congress used no such language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative prudence—practical necessity of completing the scientific predicate before standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Because an affirmative cause-or-contribute/endangerment finding is a legal predicate to issuance of standards, agencies reasonably complete that administrative work before developing standards to avoid expending resources only to discover they lack authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical consideration supports issuing separate findings and standards in sequence; requiring simultaneity would be impractical and inefficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory history—longstanding practice of relying on prior findings
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA historically has relied on earlier findings regarding pollutants’ endangerment to support later standard-setting; such history undermines claims that §202 requires concurrent determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Tier 2 implementation and other rules where EPA summarized health impacts and relied on existing findings. Past agency practice is relevant to interpreting ambiguous statutory language and rebuts the Agency’s novel interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative statutory analysis—counterexamples from other statutes are not controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to other statutes (e.g., Clean Water Act provisions or the NAAQS program) that expressly impose multi-step or simultaneous requirements do not demonstrate §202(a) requires the same sequencing, because their texts and purposes differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Congress intends concurrency or simultaneity it uses explicit language (e.g., “simultaneously” in §109(a)(2)); absent such text in §202, EPA cannot graft those requirements onto the provision by analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: On “severing” contribution from endangerment—permissible to analyze separately
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s claim that the 2009 Finding unlawfully “severed” endangerment from standards or separated endangerment from contribution (requiring an integrated single causal-chain showing that vehicles alone cause the danger) is incorrect; statutory text, case law, and the science of air pollution permit separate scientific determinations and contribution findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Administrator need only judge that an air pollutant from a class or classes of new vehicles causes or contributes to air pollution that may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare. Courts should reject demands that EPA show vehicles alone are the sole or sufficient cause in isolation from the broader causal context.
